historical_timeline.summary: Severe childhood asthma, with night attacks and trips away to find air he could breathe.
First spectacles for near-sightedness; an asthma attack sends him to Moosehead Lake, and he begins boxing and physical training.
Father died shortly after a diagnosis of stomach cancer.
Elected to the New York State Assembly.
Fever, a leg injury, and heavy weight loss on an expedition in Brazil.
Died at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay, New York.

claims.statement: Theodore Roosevelt was born at 28 East 20th Street, New York City, on October 27, 1858.

In his autobiography Roosevelt wrote that he was a sickly, delicate boy who suffered much from asthma and frequently had to be taken away on trips to find a place where he could breathe; he remembered sitting up in bed gasping at night as a very small child.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of severe childhood asthma; the National Park Service also records frequent chronic asthma attacks in childhood.

claims.statement: When he was nearly fourteen, during an attack of asthma, he was sent alone to Moosehead Lake; after two other boys on the stage-coach easily overpowered him, he began boxing lessons and a long program of physical training, with his father's approval.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the start of the exercise program he credited with his improvement.

source_links.locator: Chapter II, The Vigor of Life

claims.statement: Roosevelt wrote that he was very near-sighted as a boy without knowing it, and that at about thirteen, after he could not read a distant billboard, he got his first pair of spectacles.

A 2015 review of the historical record in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice concluded that his respiratory problems began in early childhood, that the record gives strong evidence for poorly controlled persistent asthma, that the asthma became relatively quiet in adolescence when his exercise program began at about 12, and that he continued to have serious exacerbations in adolescence and adulthood; it found little if any support for the claim that his asthma was psychosomatic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A modern retrospective classification of a documented illness. The Theodore Roosevelt Center similarly states that his symptoms eased as he grew but that he continued to suffer from asthma throughout his life. The dates of individual adult exacerbations were not verified.

claims.statement: Roosevelt received his Bachelor of Arts degree from Harvard in June 1880 and was elected to the New York State Assembly in 1881.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used for the synthetic modern occupation.

claims.statement: His father, Theodore Roosevelt Sr., died in 1878 shortly after being diagnosed with stomach cancer.
On a 1914 expedition in Brazil he contracted what was called jungle fever, injured his leg, and lost sixty pounds.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index age; recorded in the historical timeline only.

claims.statement: Roosevelt died on January 6, 1919, at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay, New York, at 60; the National Park Service attributes his death to a blood clot that had lodged in his heart.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The contemporary account does not establish whether the clot was a pulmonary embolism or a coronary event; it is reported as written.

documentation.chief_complaint: Four-week asthma review after starting maintenance-and-reliever therapy

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roosevelt returns four weeks after changing from albuterol alone to budesonide-formoterol two inhalations twice daily plus one as needed. He is much better: daytime symptoms on two or three days a week instead of most days, night waking once in four weeks, and he finishes his boxing rounds. He has used 4 to 6 as-needed inhalations a week, mostly before training. The dose counter matches about 90 percent of maintenance doses; he missed some evening doses on late session nights. His home peak flow ranges from 560 to 600 L/min. He has had no hoarseness or sore mouth. He still hopes training alone will eventually be enough. He saw the pulmonologist this morning.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roosevelt returns for his six-month review. Six weeks ago he had a moderate exacerbation with a cold, treated at a same-day visit with five days of prednisone 40 mg. The nurse telephone check three days later found his peak flow back above 500 L/min. He was not seen in clinic within the week afterwards, as his plan advised, because the appointment was never booked. He recovered fully within ten days and returned to training after two weeks. Since then he has had no night waking, no daytime symptoms apart from before training, and peak flows of 580 to 610 L/min. He takes every maintenance dose.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Roosevelt is a 23-year-old man with moderate persistent asthma, well controlled since spring on budesonide-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy (two inhalations twice daily plus as needed), who asked for a same-day visit. Three days ago he developed a runny nose and sore throat after a week of late sessions; a colleague had a cold. Since yesterday he has had wheeze, chest tightness, and a dry cough that woke him twice last night. He followed the yellow zone of his action plan: he has taken 8 reliever inhalations a day on top of his maintenance doses, which help for two to three hours. His home peak flow has been 400 to 440 L/min, against a personal best of 610. A home COVID-19 antigen test this morning was negative. He has not boxed or rowed for two days. He has had no fever above 37.8 °C, no chest pain, and no breathlessness at rest.

referral.question: Lifelong asthma in a 23-year-old athlete, uncontrolled on albuterol alone. Please confirm the diagnosis and severity, assess for type 2 inflammation and allergic triggers, and advise on treatment step and exercise
referral.pertinent_history: Asthma since early childhood. For several months: symptoms most days, night waking about twice a week, and albuterol use most days; one oral corticosteroid course at urgent care in the winter. Asthma Control Test 13. Spirometry today: FEV1 3.20 L (72 percent predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.67, rising to 3.74 L after bronchodilator (17 percent, 540 mL). Never smoker; no occupational exposure; older carpeted apartment. Boxes, rows, and takes long hill walks. Albuterol was stopped today and budesonide-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy started at two inhalations twice daily plus one as needed
questions: Do you agree that this is moderate persistent asthma, and is anything else, such as vocal cord dysfunction, contributing?
Is there evidence of type 2 or allergic inflammation, and which allergen measures are worthwhile?
Is Step 4 maintenance-and-reliever therapy the right level, and when should we step down?
How should he manage symptoms during boxing and rowing?
Is he a candidate for allergen immunotherapy or a biologic now or later?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Roosevelt is seen at the request of Dr. Kettering four weeks after starting budesonide-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy. He describes asthma since early childhood, quiet for some years in his teens and worse again over the past winter with colds. Since starting the new inhaler his symptoms have fallen to two or three days a week and night waking to once in four weeks. Colds and dusty rooms are his triggers. He has no nasal symptoms, reflux, snoring, stridor, or episodes of sudden throat tightness with normal breathing between. He believes that hard training is what keeps his asthma in check
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Intake spirometry with bronchodilator response, the Asthma Control Test scores, and today's FeNO, blood eosinophil count, total IgE, and house dust mite specific IgE

exam.finding: Fit young man, talking easily
Normal mucosa; no polyps
No stridor at rest or on forced inspiration
A few end-expiratory wheezes on forced expiration only
Did not breathe out before the dose and held his breath for only two seconds; corrected

assessment.assessment: Confirmed: variable symptoms with reversible obstruction (17 percent and 540 mL bronchodilator response). Severity before treatment was moderate persistent by NAEPP impairment criteria (FEV1 72 percent predicted, night waking about twice a week). It is improving on Step 4 therapy, with an Asthma Control Test of 18. Nothing suggests vocal cord dysfunction

FeNO 46 ppb on inhaled corticosteroid, blood eosinophils 0.42 x10³/µL, and total IgE 260 IU/mL indicate type 2 inflammation. House dust mite specific IgE 8.4 kU/L shows sensitization that fits his symptoms in dusty rooms
Mostly a sign of incomplete control, not a separate disorder. Exercise is good for him but does not treat the airway inflammation

recommendations: Continue budesonide-formoterol two inhalations twice daily and one as needed, up to 12 inhalations a day; the corrected technique and an evening-dose reminder should close most of the remaining gap
Repeat spirometry three months after starting therapy
Consider stepping down to one inhalation twice daily after at least three months of good control with no exacerbation
One reliever inhalation 5 to 20 minutes before boxing or rowing, with a proper warm-up; keep training
Dust-mite-impermeable mattress and pillow covers and weekly hot washing of bedding, since sensitization is documented
Allergen immunotherapy is not needed while asthma is controlled; reconsider if dust-mite-related symptoms persist once control is stable. A biologic is not indicated, because the asthma is not severe
PCV20 today for chronic lung disease, a yearly influenza vaccine, and a COVID-19 vaccine by CDC guidance

consultant_note.follow_up: Primary care will continue monitoring on the CMID schedule. Pulmonology will see him again for an exacerbation needing emergency care, two or more oral corticosteroid courses in a year while on treatment, or loss of control despite good adherence and technique
